column1: AP CYBER QOTD HUB - SKELETON (placeholder questions)
Three modes, one tagged pool, no next-day lock:
1. Today's Question   - date-seeded, deterministic permutation, FEATURED items only, rotates daily
2. Practice           - random from a unit, or random from anywhere, ""draw another""
3. Browse by Unit/Topic - the teacher preview, with Preview/Retrieval label + prior-topic toggle
SEO note: this hub is the NAVIGATION layer. In production each question is also its own
server-rendered, indexable page at /blogs/ap-cyber-daily-practice/{slug}. Every pool item
carries a slug + permalink so that surface exists from day one
generated when the real bank lands (lesson-pipeline render target). The hub links to them.
ENCODING: this file is intentionally ASCII-only (no emoji, no curly quotes, no bullet glyphs)
so Shopify import cannot produce mojibake. Use HTML entities only if a glyph is ever needed.
COLOR LOCK: everything is scoped under #cyb-qotd, with !important + -webkit-text-fill-color on
all colored text and buttons, and :link/:visited fixes, so Shopify's theme cannot repaint it.
font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif

column1: {""id"": ""C1-105"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.1"", ""tags"": [""spear-phishing"", ""whaling""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-researches-a-company-s-cfo-on"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker researches a company's CFO on social media, then sends that CFO a personalized email impersonating the CEO and requesting an urgent wire transfer. This attack is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""Whaling"", ""Mass phishing"", ""Baiting"", ""Quid pro quo""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Targeting a specific high-value executive (the CFO) with a tailored message is whaling, a form of spear phishing aimed at 'big fish.' Mass phishing is untargeted, baiting offers a lure item, and quid pro quo offers a service in exchange for information.""},

{""id"": ""C1-106"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.1"", ""tags"": [""pretexting"", ""response""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-worker-at-a-help-desk-gets-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A worker at a help desk gets a call: 'Hi, this is Dana from the third-floor accounting team. I'm locked out before a big deadline and my manager said you could reset my password right now.' What is the MOST appropriate response?"", ""options"": [""Reset the password immediately since a manager authorized it"", ""Ask the caller to confirm the manager's name, then reset the password"", ""Email the new temporary password to the address the caller provides"", ""Verify the caller's identity through an independent, established channel before taking action""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""The scenario is textbook pretexting. Identity must be confirmed through an independent verified channel (e.g., calling the employee back at a known number), not by trusting unverifiable claims the caller supplies. Confirming a manager's name or emailing a password the caller dictates still relies on attacker-supplied data.""},

{""id"": ""C1-107"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.1"", ""tags"": [""baiting""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-leaves-usb-drives-labeled-q4-layoffs"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker leaves USB drives labeled 'Q4 Layoffs - Confidential' in an office parking lot, hoping employees will plug them into work computers. This technique is called:"", ""options"": [""Tailgating"", ""Vishing"", ""Baiting"", ""Shoulder surfing""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Baiting lures a victim with an enticing physical or digital item (here, a curiosity-provoking USB drive) that delivers malware when used. Tailgating is following someone through a door, vishing is voice phishing, and shoulder surfing is observing credentials directly.""},

{""id"": ""C1-108"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.1"", ""tags"": [""social-engineering"", ""policy""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""a-company-adopts-the-anti-social-engineering-rules-below-which"", ""code"": ""I.   Never share passwords over phone or email
II.  Verify unexpected requests through a second channel
III. Trust any request that includes a manager's name
IV.  Report suspicious messages to the security team"", ""stem"": ""A company adopts the anti-social-engineering rules below. Which rule is itself a SECURITY WEAKNESS rather than a protection?"", ""options"": [""Rule I"", ""Rule II"", ""Rule IV"", ""Rule III""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Rule III is the weakness: a manager's name is information an attacker can easily learn and supply, so treating its mere mention as proof of legitimacy enables pretexting. The other three are sound practices.""},

{""id"": ""C1-109"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.1"", ""tags"": [""quid-pro-quo""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-cold-calls-random-employees-offering-free-tech"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker cold-calls random employees offering 'free tech support' and walks each one through steps that quietly disable their antivirus. The exchange of a supposed service for access defines which technique?"", ""options"": [""Whaling"", ""Quid pro quo"", ""Pharming"", ""Tailgating""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Quid pro quo trades a benefit (free support) for access or information. Whaling targets executives, pharming redirects traffic via DNS/host manipulation, and tailgating is unauthorized physical entry.""},

{""id"": ""C1-110"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.2"", ""tags"": [""login-anomaly"", ""impossible-travel""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-user-s-account-login-history-is-shown"", ""code"": ""Entry  Date/Time          Device        IP Location

{""id"": ""C1-111"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.2"", ""tags"": [""credential-stuffing""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-takes-username-password-pairs-leaked-from"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker takes username/password pairs leaked from one breached website and automatically tries them on many other sites. This attack is called:"", ""options"": [""Credential stuffing"", ""Brute-force cracking"", ""Keylogging"", ""Session fixation""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Credential stuffing reuses known username/password pairs across multiple services, exploiting password reuse. {""id"": ""C1-112"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.2"", ""tags"": [""login-indicators""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""while-reviewing-a-login-log-which-of-the"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""While reviewing a login log, which of the following SHOULD raise suspicion of unauthorized access?

I.   A successful login from a country the user has never visited
II.  Dozens of failed logins followed by one success
III. A login from the user's usual device and location"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""A login from a never-visited country (I) and a burst of failures ending in success (II, the signature of a successful guessing or stuffing attack) are both suspicious. {""id"": ""C1-113"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.2"", ""tags"": [""mfa"", ""mitigation""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-control-most-directly-limits-the-damage-of"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which control most directly limits the damage of stolen passwords by requiring a second proof of identity at login?"", ""options"": [""A longer password expiration window"", ""Multi-factor authentication"", ""Disabling the account lockout policy"", ""Storing passwords in the browser""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Multi-factor authentication requires a second factor (something you have or are), so a stolen password alone is insufficient. Longer expiration and disabling lockout weaken security, and browser storage does not add an authentication factor.""},

{""id"": ""C1-114"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.2"", ""tags"": [""password-practices""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-user-follows-the-habits-below-to-manage"", ""code"": ""I.   Uses a unique password for each site
II.  Reuses one strong password everywhere
III. Enables multi-factor authentication
IV.  Reviews login alerts when they arrive"", ""stem"": ""A user follows the habits below to manage account logins. Which habit MOST increases the risk that one breach compromises many accounts?"", ""options"": [""Habit I"", ""Habit II"", ""Habit III"", ""Habit IV""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Reusing one password (II) means a single leak lets attackers into every account via credential stuffing - the password's strength does not matter once it is exposed. Unique passwords, MFA, and reviewing alerts all reduce risk.""},

{""id"": ""C1-115"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.2"", ""tags"": [""response"", ""account-compromise""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-user-receives-a-real-alert-that-their"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A user receives a real alert that their email was accessed from an unrecognized device in another country. What should they do FIRST?"", ""options"": [""Delete the alert so it does not cause panic"", ""Reply to the alert email asking who logged in"", ""Wait to see whether any further alerts arrive"", ""Change the account password and sign out all active sessions""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Changing the password and terminating active sessions immediately revokes the intruder's access. Deleting or ignoring the alert leaves the attacker in, and replying to an alert email risks engaging an attacker if the alert itself is spoofed.""},

{""id"": ""C1-116"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.3"", ""tags"": [""evil-twin"", ""captive-portal""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""at-a-coffee-shop-a-laptop-shows-two"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""At a coffee shop, a laptop shows two networks: 'Sunshine Coffee' and 'Sunshine Coffee Free WiFi.' Connecting to the second opens a portal asking for an email and password to 'log in for free access.' What is the MOST likely threat?"", ""options"": [""A legitimate captive portal that is always safe to use"", ""An evil twin access point harvesting credentials through a fake portal"", ""A firewall blocking the real network"", ""A VPN automatically protecting the connection""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""A second, similarly named network paired with a credential-harvesting portal is a classic evil twin: an attacker-run access point that mimics the real one to capture logins. A genuine portal would not need account credentials, and no VPN or firewall is implied.""},

{""id"": ""C1-117"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.3"", ""tags"": [""public-wifi"", ""vpn""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-does-using-a-vpn-on-public-wi-fi"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why does using a VPN on public Wi-Fi improve security even when the network itself is untrusted?"", ""options"": [""It hides the device from all other users on the network entirely and physically"", ""It encrypts the device's traffic so others on the network cannot read it"", ""It removes the need for any website to use HTTPS"", ""It guarantees the website being visited is legitimate""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""A VPN encrypts traffic between the device and the VPN server, so eavesdroppers on the shared network see only ciphertext. It does not make the device invisible, replace HTTPS, or verify a destination site's legitimacy.""},

{""id"": ""C1-118"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.3"", ""tags"": [""public-network-practices""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-practices-reduce-risk-when-using-public-wi-fi"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which practices reduce risk when using public Wi-Fi?

I.   Confirming the official network name with staff before connecting
II.  Verifying that sites show HTTPS before entering credentials
III. Enabling file sharing so colleagues can reach your device"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Confirming the legitimate network name (I) avoids evil twins, and requiring HTTPS (II) protects data in transit. Enabling file sharing on an untrusted network (III) exposes the device to other users and increases risk.""},

{""id"": ""C1-119"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.3"", ""tags"": [""public-network-habits""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-traveler-does-the-following-on-airport-wi-fi"", ""code"": ""I.   Reads news on an HTTPS site

III. Uses a VPN before browsing

Which action is the RISKIEST?"", ""options"": [""Action II"", ""Action I"", ""Action III"", ""Action IV""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Logging into banking over open Wi-Fi (II) exposes high-value credentials to potential eavesdropping or an evil twin, especially without a VPN. {""id"": ""C1-120"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.3"", ""tags"": [""man-in-the-middle""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""on-an-open-wireless-network-with-no-encryption"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""On an open wireless network with no encryption, an attacker positions themselves between a user and the gateway to intercept and possibly alter traffic. This is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""A denial-of-service attack"", ""A man-in-the-middle attack"", ""A SQL injection"", ""A brute-force attack""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Intercepting (and potentially modifying) traffic between two parties is a man-in-the-middle attack, which open networks make easy. Denial of service blocks availability, SQL injection targets databases, and brute force guesses credentials.""},

{""id"": ""C1-121"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.4"", ""tags"": [""ai-phishing"", ""scale""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""how-do-ai-tools-most-significantly-change-the"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""How do AI tools most significantly change the threat posed by phishing campaigns?"", ""options"": [""They let attackers generate large volumes of personalized, fluent messages quickly"", ""They make all phishing emails contain obvious spelling errors"", ""They eliminate the need for a victim to click anything"", ""They prevent email providers from filtering spam""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""AI lets attackers produce many highly personalized, grammatically clean messages at scale, raising both volume and believability. It does not introduce errors, remove the need for victim interaction, or disable spam filters.""},

{""id"": ""C1-122"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.4"", ""tags"": [""deepfake"", ""voice-cloning""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-employee-receives-a-phone-call-that-sounds"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An employee receives a phone call that sounds exactly like their manager's voice, urgently asking them to approve a payment. The 'manager' is later found to have made no such call. Which AI-enabled attack is MOST consistent with this?"", ""options"": [""A SQL injection"", ""A brute-force password attack"", ""AI-generated voice cloning (audio deepfake)"", ""A captive portal attack""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""AI voice cloning can synthesize a convincing imitation of a known person's voice to authorize fraudulent actions. The other options describe database, password, and network attacks unrelated to synthetic audio.""},

{""id"": ""C1-123"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.4"", ""tags"": [""ai-attacks"", ""characteristics""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""which-statements-about-ai-based-cyberattacks-are-true-i"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which statements about AI-based cyberattacks are TRUE?

I.   AI can generate deepfake audio and video to impersonate real people
II.  AI lowers the skill and time needed to launch convincing attacks at scale
III. AI-generated phishing is always easy to detect because it sounds robotic"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III"", ""I and II only""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""AI can fabricate realistic audio/video impersonations (I) and reduce the effort to scale convincing attacks (II). Statement III is false: modern AI text is fluent and natural, making AI phishing harder, not easier, to spot.""},

{""id"": ""C1-124"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.4"", ""tags"": [""deepfake"", ""verification""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""after-a-deepfake-voice-scam-a-team-proposes"", ""code"": ""I.   Confirm money transfers through a pre-agreed code word
II.  Trust any request if the caller's voice sounds correct
III. Call the requester back on a known, official number
IV.  Require a second approver for large transfers"", ""stem"": ""After a deepfake voice scam, a team proposes new verification rules. Which proposed rule would FAIL to defend against a convincing voice clone?"", ""options"": [""Rule I"", ""Rule III"", ""Rule II"", ""Rule IV""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Rule II fails because the entire danger of voice cloning is that the voice sounds correct, so it cannot be the test. {""id"": ""C1-125"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.5"", ""tags"": [""anomaly-detection""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-security-system-uses-ai-to-learn-each"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A security system uses AI to learn each user's normal login times, locations, and devices, then flags logins that deviate sharply from that pattern. This defensive technique is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""Anomaly (behavior-based) detection"", ""Signature-based filtering"", ""Password hashing"", ""Physical access control""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Learning a baseline of normal behavior and flagging deviations is anomaly/behavior-based detection. Signature-based filtering matches known patterns, hashing protects stored passwords, and physical access control governs entry to spaces.""},

{""id"": ""C1-126"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.5"", ""tags"": [""ai-defense"", ""uses""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-are-legitimate-ways-ai-helps-defenders-i"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which are legitimate ways AI helps defenders?

I.   Detecting unusual account behavior faster than manual review
II.  Triaging large volumes of alerts to surface likely threats
III. Guaranteeing zero false positives in threat detection"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I and II only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""AI excels at rapidly spotting anomalies (I) and prioritizing high volumes of alerts (II). Statement III is false: AI systems still produce false positives and false negatives and cannot guarantee perfect accuracy.""},

{""id"": ""C1-127"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.5"", ""tags"": [""ai-defense"", ""limitations""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""which-statement-best-describes-a-key-limitation-of"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which statement BEST describes a key limitation of relying on AI for cyber defense?"", ""options"": [""AI defenses make human oversight completely unnecessary"", ""AI defenses can produce false positives and may miss novel attacks not reflected in their training"", ""AI defenses can detect only attacks that have already been publicly reported"", ""AI defenses cannot process more data than a human analyst""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""AI defenses can misclassify benign activity (false positives) and may fail on truly novel attacks outside their learned patterns, so human oversight remains important. They do process more data than humans and are not limited to publicly reported attacks.""},

{""id"": ""C1-128"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.5"", ""tags"": [""ai-defense"", ""false-positive""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-ai-monitoring-tool-flags-a-finance-employee"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An AI monitoring tool flags a finance employee's first-ever late-night login from a new laptop as suspicious, but it turns out the employee simply bought a new computer and worked late. This outcome is an example of:"", ""options"": [""A false positive"", ""A false negative"", ""A zero-day exploit"", ""A denial-of-service event""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""The system raised an alarm for legitimate activity, which is a false positive. A false negative would be missing a real attack
column2: the other options are unrelated attack types.""},

column1: {""id"": ""C1-129"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.5"", ""tags"": [""ai-defense"", ""human-in-loop""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-is-human-review-still-important-even-when"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why is human review still important even when AI handles most threat detection?"", ""options"": [""Humans can read encrypted traffic that AI cannot"", ""AI is unable to process more than one alert at a time"", ""Humans never make mistakes in security decisions"", ""Humans can investigate flagged events in context and catch AI errors""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Humans add contextual judgment and can correct AI mistakes such as false positives or missed novel attacks. AI handles high volume well, neither humans nor AI read properly encrypted traffic without keys, and humans are certainly not error-free.""},

{""id"": ""C1-130"", ""unit"": 1, ""topic"": ""1.4"", ""tags"": [""1.5"", ""ai-dual-use""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""ai-is-described-as-dual-use-in-cybersecurity-which"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""AI is described as 'dual-use' in cybersecurity. Which statements support this characterization?

I.   The same generative models that scale phishing can also draft user-awareness training

III. AI is useful only to attackers, never to defenders"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Dual-use means the same capabilities aid both sides: generative models help attackers and defenders (I), and behavioral modeling can be turned to evasion (II). Statement III is false because AI clearly benefits defenders as well.""},

{""id"": ""C2-101"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""cia-triad"", ""integrity""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-hospital-discovers-that-a-patient-s-recorded"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A hospital discovers that a patient's recorded blood type was silently altered in its database. Which element of the CIA triad was MOST directly violated?"", ""options"": [""Confidentiality"", ""Availability"", ""Authentication"", ""Integrity""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Unauthorized alteration of data violates integrity, which concerns accuracy and trustworthiness. {""id"": ""C2-102"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""cia-triad"", ""availability""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-ransomware-attack-encrypts-a-company-s-files"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A ransomware attack encrypts a company's files so employees cannot open them until a ransom is paid. Which element of the CIA triad is MOST directly affected?"", ""options"": [""Confidentiality"", ""Availability"", ""Integrity"", ""Non-repudiation""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Blocking legitimate users from accessing their own data primarily harms availability. The data may still be confidential and unaltered

{""id"": ""C2-103"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""risk"", ""definitions""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""consider-these-definitions-used-in-risk-analysis-which"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Consider these definitions used in risk analysis. column1: {""id"": ""C2-104"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""least-privilege""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-new-intern-is-given-access-only-to"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A new intern is given access only to the specific shared folder needed for their project and nothing more. This BEST illustrates which principle?"", ""options"": [""Least privilege"", ""Defense in depth"", ""Security through obscurity"", ""Non-repudiation""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Granting only the minimum access required for a role is the principle of least privilege. Defense in depth layers multiple controls, security through obscurity hides design details, and non-repudiation ensures actions cannot be denied.""},

{""id"": ""C2-105"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""defense-in-depth""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-building-uses-a-perimeter-fence-a-badge-controlled"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A building uses a perimeter fence, a badge-controlled lobby, a locked server room, and a logged cabinet for backups. Relying on multiple independent layers so that no single failure grants full access BEST illustrates:"", ""options"": [""Least privilege"", ""Single sign-on"", ""Separation of duties"", ""Defense in depth""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Layering several independent controls so a breach of one does not compromise everything is defense in depth. Least privilege limits access scope, single sign-on consolidates logins, and separation of duties divides a task among people.""},

{""id"": ""C2-106"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""control-types""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""a-team-labels-each-control-by-its-function"", ""code"": ""I.   Security camera footage reviewed after an incident - detective

column1: {""id"": ""C2-107"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""control-categories""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-written-acceptable-use-policy-that-employees-must-sign"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A written acceptable-use policy that employees must sign is BEST categorized as which type of control?"", ""options"": [""Administrative control"", ""Physical control"", ""Technical control"", ""Biometric control""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Policies, procedures, and training are administrative (managerial) controls. {""id"": ""C2-108"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""tailgating""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-employee-badges-into-a-secure-door-and"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An employee badges into a secure door and an unfamiliar person carrying a large box says 'Could you hold that? The other options are digital attacks unrelated to physical entry.""},

{""id"": ""C2-109"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""dumpster-diving""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-recovers-printed-account-statements-and-an"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker recovers printed account statements and an org chart from a company's unsecured trash bins to plan a later attack. {""id"": ""C2-110"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""shoulder-surfing""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-person-standing-close-behind-a-user-at"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A person standing close behind a user at an ATM watches them enter their PIN. This is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""Baiting"", ""A watering hole attack"", ""Pretexting"", ""Shoulder surfing""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Directly observing someone enter sensitive information is shoulder surfing. {""id"": ""C2-111"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""physical-attacks""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-of-the-following-are-physical-security-threats"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which of the following are physical security threats rather than purely digital ones?

III. A SQL injection against a web form"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I and II only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Tailgating (I) and laptop theft (II) are physical threats. SQL injection (III) is a software/application attack carried out over a network, not a physical one.""},

{""id"": ""C2-112"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""clean-desk""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-office-reviews-employee-habits-which-habit-creates"", ""code"": ""I.   Locks the screen when stepping away

Locking screens, shredding sensitive documents, and securing backups all reduce risk.""},

{""id"": ""C2-113"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.3"", ""tags"": [""mantrap-tailgating""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""to-stop-tailgating-at-a-data-center-entrance"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""To stop tailgating at a data center entrance, which control is MOST effective because it allows only one authenticated person to pass at a time?"", ""options"": [""A motion-activated camera"", ""A visitor sign-in sheet"", ""A taller perimeter fence"", ""An access-control vestibule (mantrap)""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""An access-control vestibule (mantrap) physically allows only one verified person through per cycle, directly preventing piggybacking. A camera detects but does not prevent, a sign-in sheet relies on honesty, and a fence does not address a person following through a door.""},

{""id"": ""C2-114"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.3"", ""tags"": [""biometrics""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-fingerprint-scanner-at-a-secure-door-authenticates"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A fingerprint scanner at a secure door authenticates people based on:"", ""options"": [""Something you know"", ""Something you are"", ""Something you have"", ""Somewhere you are""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Biometrics such as fingerprints are 'something you are.' {""id"": ""C2-115"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.3"", ""tags"": [""physical-controls""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-controls-help-protect-a-physical-server-room"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which controls help protect a physical server room?

{""id"": ""C2-116"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.3"", ""tags"": [""least-privilege-physical""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-company-gives-every-employee-a-master-badge"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A company gives every employee a master badge that opens all doors 'for convenience.' {""id"": ""C2-118"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.4"", ""tags"": [""detection-vs-prevention""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""surveillance-cameras-that-record-activity-in-a-parking"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Surveillance cameras that record activity in a parking garage are PRIMARILY which kind of control?"", ""options"": [""Preventive"", ""Corrective"", ""Detective"", ""Compensating only""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Cameras that record events support detection and later investigation, making them detective controls. {""id"": ""C2-119"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.4"", ""tags"": [""detection-methods""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-mechanisms-help-detect-a-physical-intrusion-as"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which mechanisms help DETECT a physical intrusion (as opposed to preventing one)?

I.   Motion sensors that trigger an alert
II.  Entry logs reviewed for unusual access times
III. A deadbolt lock on the door"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Motion sensors (I) and reviewed entry logs (II) reveal that an intrusion occurred. A deadbolt (III) prevents entry
column2: it does not detect or report an attempt.""},

column1: {""id"": ""C2-120"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.4"", ""tags"": [""audit-log""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""reviewing-a-door-access-log-security-notices-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Reviewing a door access log, security notices a badge belonging to an employee on vacation entered the records room at 2:00 AM. Dismissing the log or assuming benign explanations ignores a clear anomaly.""},

{""id"": ""C2-121"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.4"", ""tags"": [""alarm-response""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-is-an-intrusion-alarm-more-useful-when"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why is an intrusion alarm more useful when paired with a defined response procedure?"", ""options"": [""The alarm becomes a preventive control on its own"", ""It removes the need for any physical locks"", ""Detection only reduces harm if someone acts on the alert"", ""It guarantees no false alarms""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Detection has value only if it leads to action
column2: a response procedure ensures alerts are investigated and contained. An alarm does not become preventive by itself, does not replace locks, and does not eliminate false alarms.""},

column1: {""id"": ""C2-122"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""2.4"", ""control-functions""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""a-guard-checks-ids-at-the-door-stopping"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A guard checks IDs at the door (stopping unauthorized entry) AND patrols hallways to spot and report break-ins. The guard is therefore serving as which combination of controls?"", ""options"": [""Preventive and detective"", ""Corrective and compensating"", ""Detective only"", ""Preventive only""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Checking IDs prevents unauthorized entry (preventive) while patrolling to spot and report intrusions detects them (detective). The guard fills both roles, so neither single-function answer is complete.""},

{""id"": ""C2-123"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""cia-mapping""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""match-each-safeguard-to-the-cia-element-it"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Match each safeguard to the CIA element it most directly supports. All three pairings are correct.""},

{""id"": ""C2-124"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""2.3"", ""visitor-policy""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-site-s-visitor-policy-contains-the-rules"", ""code"": ""I.   Visitors sign in and wear a temporary badge

Sign-in with badges, escorting visitors, and expiring badges are all sound practices.""},

{""id"": ""C2-125"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""risk-treatment""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-company-decides-the-cost-of-a-control"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A company decides the cost of a control exceeds the expected loss from a low-probability threat, so it formally chooses to accept that residual risk. This risk response is BEST called:"", ""options"": [""Risk avoidance"", ""Risk acceptance"", ""Risk transfer"", ""Risk elimination""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Knowingly choosing to tolerate a risk because mitigation is not cost-effective is risk acceptance. Avoidance removes the activity, transfer shifts the risk (e.g., insurance), and risk can rarely be fully eliminated.""},

{""id"": ""C2-126"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.2"", ""tags"": [""2.4"", ""combined""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""after-hours-footage-shows-an-unknown-person-tailgating-through"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""After-hours footage shows an unknown person tailgating through the lobby, then the records-room door log shows an entry with no matching badge swipe seconds later. Deleting evidence, dismissing a public lobby, or assuming authorization all ignore the anomaly.""},

{""id"": ""C2-127"", ""unit"": 2, ""topic"": ""2.1"", ""tags"": [""threat-vs-vulnerability""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-unlocked-back-door-is-best-described-as"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An unlocked back door is BEST described as which of the following, and an intruder who wants to use it is which?"", ""options"": [""The unlocked door is a threat

column1: {""id"": ""C3-101"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.1"", ""tags"": [""ddos""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-website-becomes-unreachable-because-thousands-of-compromised"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A website becomes unreachable because thousands of compromised devices flood it with traffic simultaneously. {""id"": ""C3-102"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.1"", ""tags"": [""packet-sniffing""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""on-an-unencrypted-network-an-attacker-captures-and"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""On an unencrypted network, an attacker captures and reads packets passing across the wire, including a plaintext login. DoS disrupts availability, ARP poisoning manipulates address mappings, and brute force guesses credentials.""},

{""id"": ""C3-103"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.1"", ""tags"": [""spoofing""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-forges-the-source-ip-address-of"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker forges the source IP address of packets so they appear to come from a trusted internal host. {""id"": ""C3-107"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.2"", ""tags"": [""wireless-encryption""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-wireless-configuration-provides-the-strongest-protection-for"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which wireless configuration provides the STRONGEST protection for a modern office Wi-Fi network?"", ""options"": [""An open network with no password"", ""WEP encryption"", ""WPA3 encryption"", ""Hiding the SSID with no encryption""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""WPA3 is the current strong standard for Wi-Fi encryption. {""id"": ""C3-108"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.2"", ""tags"": [""wireless-config""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-office-configures-its-wireless-network-with-the"", ""code"": ""I.   Uses WPA2/WPA3 encryption

{""id"": ""C3-109"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.2"", ""tags"": [""managerial-controls""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-written-policy-requiring-employees-to-connect-personal"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A written policy requiring employees to connect personal devices only to a separate guest network is an example of which control category?"", ""options"": [""Technical control"", ""Managerial (administrative) control"", ""Physical control"", ""Biometric control""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Policies and procedures are managerial/administrative controls. {""id"": ""C3-112"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.3"", ""tags"": [""dmz""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-company-places-its-public-web-server-in"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A company places its public web server in a DMZ between the internet and its internal network. {""id"": ""C3-117"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.4"", ""tags"": [""firewall-scope""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-statement-best-describes-what-a-network-firewall"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which statement BEST describes what a network firewall does?"", ""options"": [""It scans email attachments for spelling errors"", ""It filters traffic between networks based on a set of rules"", ""It encrypts every file stored on a hard drive"", ""It physically prevents people from entering a server room""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""A firewall enforces rules that permit or block traffic between networks or hosts. {""id"": ""C3-118"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.4"", ""tags"": [""firewall-limits""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-statements-about-firewalls-are-true-i-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which statements about firewalls are TRUE?

{""id"": ""C3-119"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""ids-vs-ips""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""what-is-the-key-difference-between-an-intrusion"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""What is the KEY difference between an intrusion detection system (IDS) and an intrusion prevention system (IPS)?"", ""options"": [""An IDS alerts on suspicious traffic
column2: an IPS can also actively block it"", ""An IDS encrypts traffic
column3: an IPS decrypts it"", ""An IDS works only on wireless
column4: an IPS works only on wired networks"", ""There is no functional difference between them""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""An IDS monitors and alerts on suspicious activity, while an IPS additionally takes action to block or drop malicious traffic in line. column1: {""id"": ""C3-120"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""signature-vs-anomaly""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-detection-system-that-compares-traffic-against-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A detection system that compares traffic against a database of known attack patterns uses which method, and what is its main weakness?"", ""options"": [""Anomaly-based
column2: it cannot detect any known attacks"", ""Signature-based
column3: it produces no false negatives ever"", ""Signature-based
column4: it may miss brand-new attacks not yet in its database"", ""Anomaly-based
column5: it requires no baseline of normal behavior""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Matching traffic to known patterns is signature-based detection, whose weakness is missing novel (zero-day) attacks absent from its signature database. Anomaly-based detection instead learns a baseline and flags deviations.""},

column1: {""id"": ""C3-121"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""siem""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-siem-system-aggregates-logs-from-firewalls-servers"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A SIEM system aggregates logs from firewalls, servers, and IDS sensors, then correlates events to highlight likely incidents. Its PRIMARY value is that it:"", ""options"": [""Replaces the need for firewalls and IDS sensors"", ""Centralizes and correlates data from many sources to reveal patterns a single log would miss"", ""Encrypts all network traffic end to end"", ""Physically secures the data center""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""A SIEM centralizes and correlates events across many sources so that distributed attack patterns become visible. It complements rather than replaces firewalls and IDS, does not perform traffic encryption, and is unrelated to physical security.""},

{""id"": ""C3-122"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""detection-concepts""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""which-statements-about-detecting-network-attacks-are-true"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which statements about detecting network attacks are TRUE?

I.   Signature-based detection struggles with zero-day attacks
II.  Anomaly-based detection can generate false positives from unusual but benign activity
III. A SIEM helps correlate events from multiple devices"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""I, II, and III"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Signature detection misses unknown attacks (I), anomaly detection can flag harmless oddities as false positives (II), and a SIEM correlates multi-source events (III). All three statements are true.""},

{""id"": ""C3-123"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""log-analysis""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-siem-correlates-these-near-simultaneous-events-hundreds-of"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A SIEM correlates these near-simultaneous events: hundreds of failed logins on a server, one success, then a large outbound data transfer to an unfamiliar IP. Routine backups, simple mistyping, and updates would not produce this exact correlated pattern.""},

{""id"": ""C3-124"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""monitoring-gaps""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-organization-s-network-monitoring-setup-is-described-below"", ""code"": ""I.   IDS sensors watch inbound traffic

Watching inbound traffic, feeding logs to a SIEM, and automated correlation are all strengths, not gaps.""},

{""id"": ""C3-125"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.5"", ""tags"": [""baseline""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-does-anomaly-based-network-detection-require-establishing-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why does anomaly-based network detection require establishing a baseline of normal activity first?"", ""options"": [""To know what 'unusual' looks like so deviations can be flagged"", ""To encrypt all traffic on the network"", ""To replace the firewall's rule set"", ""To physically lock the network closet""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Anomaly detection flags deviations from normal, so it must first learn what normal looks like. It is not an encryption, firewall, or physical-security mechanism.""},

{""id"": ""C3-126"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.1"", ""tags"": [""3.4"", ""attack-defense-map""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""match-each-attack-to-a-control-that-helps"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Match each attack to a control that helps defend against it. {""id"": ""C3-127"", ""unit"": 3, ""topic"": ""3.1"", ""tags"": [""dos-vs-ddos""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""why-is-a-distributed-denial-of-service-ddos-attack-typically"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack typically HARDER to defend against than a single-source denial-of-service attack?"", ""options"": [""DDoS traffic is always encrypted and unreadable"", ""Traffic comes from many distributed sources, so simply blocking one address is insufficient"", ""DDoS attacks only target wireless networks"", ""A single firewall rule always stops a DDoS completely""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""DDoS traffic originates from many distributed hosts, so blocking a single source does little

{""id"": ""C4-104"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.1"", ""tags"": [""iot"", ""default-credentials""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-company-installs-internet-connected-security-cameras-but-never"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A company installs internet-connected security cameras but never changes the manufacturer's default admin password. {""id"": ""C4-106"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.1"", ""tags"": [""zero-day""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""a-zero-day-vulnerability-is-best-described-as-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A zero-day vulnerability is BEST described as a flaw that:"", ""options"": [""Has been known and patched for years"", ""Can only affect devices that are turned off"", ""Is unknown to the vendor or unpatched, so no fix is yet available"", ""Exists only in printed manuals""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""A zero-day is a vulnerability with no available patch because the vendor has not yet fixed (or learned of) it, giving defenders 'zero days' to prepare. {""id"": ""C4-108"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.2"", ""tags"": [""mfa-factors""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-login-that-requires-a-password-plus-a"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A login that requires a password PLUS a code from the user's phone combines which two authentication factors?"", ""options"": [""Something you are and somewhere you are"", ""Something you know and something you have"", ""Something you have and something you are"", ""Two instances of something you know""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""A password is something you know and a code on the user's phone is something you have, so this combines two distinct factor types - true multi-factor authentication. A biometric would be 'something you are.'""},

{""id"": ""C4-109"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.2"", ""tags"": [""mfa-misconception""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-site-claims-to-use-multi-factor-authentication-which"", ""code"": ""I.   Password plus a fingerprint scan
II.  Password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app
III. Password plus a second, different password
IV.  PIN plus a hardware security key"", ""stem"": ""A site claims to use multi-factor authentication. Which described login is NOT genuine multi-factor authentication?"", ""options"": [""Login I"", ""Login II"", ""Login III"", ""Login IV""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""A password plus another password (III) uses two instances of the same factor (something you know), so it is not true multi-factor. The others each combine two different factor types.""},

{""id"": ""C4-110"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.2"", ""tags"": [""password-manager""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-does-using-a-password-manager-improve-account"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why does using a password manager improve account security?"", ""options"": [""It lets users keep one easy password for every site"", ""It makes multi-factor authentication unnecessary"", ""It enables a unique, strong password per site without memorizing them all"", ""It publicly shares passwords for backup""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""A password manager generates and stores a unique strong password for each site, defeating credential-stuffing risk from reuse, without the user memorizing them. It does not encourage reuse, replace MFA, or share passwords publicly.""},

{""id"": ""C4-111"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.2"", ""tags"": [""password-policy""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-password-practices-strengthen-account-security-i-using"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which password practices strengthen account security?

I.   Using a long, unique passphrase per account
II.  Enabling multi-factor authentication
III. Reusing one memorable password across all accounts"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III"", ""I and II only""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Long unique passphrases (I) and MFA (II) both strengthen security. Reusing one password everywhere (III) is a weakness that lets one breach compromise every account.""},

{""id"": ""C4-112"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.2"", ""tags"": [""biometric-tradeoff""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-is-a-genuine-drawback-of-biometric-authentication"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which is a genuine drawback of biometric authentication compared with a password?"", ""options"": [""Biometrics can be changed instantly if compromised"", ""Biometrics require the user to memorize a long string"", ""Biometrics are never convenient for users"", ""A compromised biometric cannot simply be reset like a password""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Unlike a password, a fingerprint or face cannot be reissued if its data is stolen, which is a real drawback. Biometrics are generally convenient and require no memorization, so the other options are false.""},

{""id"": ""C4-113"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.3"", ""tags"": [""hardening""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""disabling-unused-services-removing-unnecessary-software-and-closing"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Disabling unused services, removing unnecessary software, and closing unneeded ports on a device is collectively known as:"", ""options"": [""Social engineering"", ""Packet sniffing"", ""Device hardening"", ""Phishing""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Reducing a device's attack surface by removing or disabling what is not needed is device hardening. The other options are attack techniques, not protective measures.""},

{""id"": ""C4-114"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.3"", ""tags"": [""ransomware-backups""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""to-minimize-damage-if-ransomware-encrypts-a-workstation"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""To minimize damage if ransomware encrypts a workstation's files, the MOST effective preparation is to:"", ""options"": [""Maintain regular, tested offline or isolated backups of important data"", ""Store the only copy of files on the same workstation"", ""Disable all software updates"", ""Use the same password everywhere for quick recovery""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Regular, tested backups kept offline or isolated let an organization restore data without paying a ransom. Keeping the only copy on the infected device, disabling updates, and reusing passwords all worsen the situation.""},

{""id"": ""C4-115"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.3"", ""tags"": [""device-protection""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-measures-help-protect-an-individual-laptop-i"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which measures help protect an individual laptop?

I.   Keeping the operating system and applications patched
II.  Encrypting the disk so a stolen drive is unreadable
III. Leaving the device unlocked for convenience"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III"", ""I and II only""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Patching (I) closes known vulnerabilities and disk encryption (II) protects data if the device is stolen. Leaving the device unlocked (III) removes a basic protection and increases risk.""},

{""id"": ""C4-116"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.3"", ""tags"": [""hardening-checklist""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""an-it-team-applies-the-hardening-steps-below"", ""code"": ""I.   Changes default administrator passwords
II.  Enables automatic security updates
III. Grants every user local administrator rights
IV.  Removes preinstalled software that is not needed"", ""stem"": ""An IT team applies the hardening steps below to new devices. Which step WEAKENS security rather than strengthening it?"", ""options"": [""Step I"", ""Step II"", ""Step IV"", ""Step III""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Giving every user local administrator rights (III) violates least privilege and lets any compromise gain full control of the device. Changing default passwords, enabling updates, and removing bloatware all harden the device.""},

{""id"": ""C4-117"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.3"", ""tags"": [""disk-encryption""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""encrypting-a-laptop-s-hard-drive-primarily-protects"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Encrypting a laptop's hard drive PRIMARILY protects against which outcome?"", ""options"": [""The laptop running out of battery"", ""A phishing email reaching the user"", ""A stolen laptop's data being read by the thief"", ""The network being flooded by a DDoS""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Full-disk encryption renders stored data unreadable to anyone without the key, protecting confidentiality if the device is lost or stolen. It does not affect battery life, email phishing, or network availability.""},

{""id"": ""C4-118"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.4"", ""tags"": [""signs-of-compromise""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-of-the-following-is-the-strongest-sign"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which of the following is the STRONGEST sign that a workstation may be infected with malware?"", ""options"": [""The screen brightness is set to maximum"", ""The user has many browser bookmarks"", ""The desktop wallpaper was recently changed by the user"", ""Unknown programs launch on startup and the device sends large amounts of unexplained network traffic""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Unknown auto-starting programs plus unexplained outbound traffic strongly indicate malware (e.g., a bot communicating with a command server). Brightness, bookmarks, and a user-chosen wallpaper are benign.""},

{""id"": ""C4-119"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.4"", ""tags"": [""edr-behavioral""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""endpoint-detection-that-watches-a-device-for-suspicious"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Endpoint detection that watches a device for suspicious BEHAVIOR (such as a program suddenly encrypting many files) rather than only matching known malware signatures is valuable because it can:"", ""options"": [""Encrypt the network connection"", ""Replace the need for backups"", ""Physically lock the device"", ""Detect novel threats that have no known signature yet""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Behavioral detection can catch new or modified malware that signature scanning would miss, by reacting to malicious actions. It does not encrypt connections, replace backups, or provide physical security.""},

{""id"": ""C4-120"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.4"", ""tags"": [""detection-signals""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-observations-could-indicate-a-device-has-been"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which observations could indicate a device has been compromised?

I.   Antivirus has been silently disabled
II.  New unknown administrator accounts appear
III. The device receives a routine vendor security patch"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I and II only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Antivirus being silently disabled (I) and unexpected new admin accounts (II) are classic indicators of compromise. Receiving a routine vendor patch (III) is normal, expected maintenance.""},

{""id"": ""C4-121"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.4"", ""tags"": [""response""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""a-user-notices-their-device-is-unusually-slow"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A user notices their device is unusually slow, a security tool reports a disabled service, and files are being renamed with a strange extension. What is the BEST immediate action?"", ""options"": [""Disconnect the device from the network and report it to security/IT"", ""Pay any ransom demand right away"", ""Keep working and hope it resolves itself"", ""Connect more devices to share the load""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""These are signs of active malware (likely ransomware)
column2: isolating the device from the network limits spread and preserves evidence while experts respond. Paying immediately, ignoring it, or connecting more devices all increase harm.""},

column1: {""id"": ""C4-122"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.4"", ""tags"": [""logs""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-are-device-and-application-logs-valuable-after"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why are device and application logs valuable AFTER a security incident?"", ""options"": [""They automatically reverse all damage"", ""They can show what happened, when, and how the attacker acted, aiding investigation"", ""They encrypt the device retroactively"", ""They prevent the attack from ever starting""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Logs provide a record that supports investigation and response after an incident. They do not undo damage, encrypt retroactively, or prevent the original attack.""},

{""id"": ""C4-123"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.4"", ""tags"": [""detection-gap""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-small-office-relies-on-the-device-security-setup"", ""code"": ""I.   Antivirus is installed on all devices

Installed antivirus, automatic updates, and nightly backups all support, not undermine, security.""},

{""id"": ""C4-124"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.1"", ""tags"": [""4.3"", ""attack-defense-map""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""match-each-device-threat-to-a-control-that"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Match each device threat to a control that helps defend against it. I.   Stolen laptop with sensitive files - full-disk encryption

III. Default device password abuse - changing default credentials"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Disk encryption protects a stolen laptop's data (I), patching closes known vulnerabilities (II), and changing default credentials prevents default-password abuse (III). All three pairings are reasonable.""},

{""id"": ""C4-125"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.1"", ""tags"": [""malware-spread""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""which-scenario-best-illustrates-why-a-single-unpatched"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which scenario BEST illustrates why a single unpatched device can endanger an entire network?"", ""options"": [""The unpatched device simply runs more slowly than the rest"", ""A worm exploits the unpatched device, then spreads automatically to others sharing the network"", ""The unpatched device uses more electricity"", ""The unpatched device displays advertisements only to its own user""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""A worm can exploit one unpatched host and self-propagate to others, so a single weak device becomes an entry point for the whole network. Slower speed, power use, and local ads do not endanger other devices.""},

{""id"": ""C4-126"", ""unit"": 4, ""topic"": ""4.2"", ""tags"": [""sso-tradeoff""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""single-sign-on-sso-lets-users-access-many-applications"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Single sign-on (SSO) lets users access many applications with one login. What is a security TRADE-OFF of SSO?"", ""options"": [""Users must memorize a separate password for every application"", ""If the single set of credentials is compromised, many applications are exposed at once"", ""It makes every application slower to load"", ""It removes the ability to log out""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""SSO concentrates risk: compromising the one credential can expose every connected application, which is why SSO is usually paired with strong MFA. SSO reduces the number of passwords to remember rather than increasing it.""},

{""id"": ""C5-101"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.1"", ""tags"": [""sql-injection""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-login-form-passes-user-input-directly-into"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A login form passes user input directly into a database query, allowing an attacker to type input that changes the query and bypasses the password check. This attack is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""A denial-of-service attack"", ""Tailgating"", ""A replay attack"", ""SQL injection""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Injecting input that alters a database query is SQL injection, caused by trusting unsanitized user input. DoS targets availability, tailgating is physical, and a replay attack resends captured traffic.""},

{""id"": ""C5-102"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.1"", ""tags"": [""xss""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""an-attacker-submits-a-comment-containing-a-script"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""An attacker submits a comment containing a script that later runs in other visitors' browsers when they view the page. This attack is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""A brute-force attack"", ""Cross-site scripting (XSS)"", ""A DDoS attack"", ""Dumpster diving""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Injecting a script that executes in other users' browsers is cross-site scripting (XSS), which results from failing to sanitize output. Brute force guesses credentials, DDoS floods availability, and dumpster diving is physical reconnaissance.""},

{""id"": ""C5-103"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.1"", ""tags"": [""root-cause""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""both-sql-injection-and-cross-site-scripting-share-which"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Both SQL injection and cross-site scripting share which common root cause?"", ""options"": [""Using too many backups"", ""Encrypting data at rest"", ""Enabling multi-factor authentication"", ""Failure to validate and sanitize untrusted input/output""], ""answer"": 3, ""explanation"": ""Both stem from trusting untrusted input/output without validation or sanitization. Backups, encryption, and MFA are protections and are not the cause of these injection flaws.""},

{""id"": ""C5-104"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.1"", ""tags"": [""app-attacks""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-of-the-following-are-application-layer-attacks-i"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which of the following are application-layer attacks?

I.   SQL injection
II.  Cross-site scripting
III. Tailgating into a server room"", ""options"": [""II and III only"", ""I and II only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""SQL injection (I) and cross-site scripting (II) target application input/output handling. Tailgating (III) is a physical security attack, not an application-layer one.""},

{""id"": ""C5-105"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.1"", ""tags"": [""broken-access-control""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""expert"", ""featured"": false, ""slug"": ""a-banking-app-shows-a-user-their-statement"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A banking app shows a user their statement at the URL .../account?id=1042. The user changes the URL to id=1043 and sees another customer's statement. Which vulnerability does this reveal?"", ""options"": [""A strong encryption scheme working correctly"", ""Broken access control (the app fails to verify the user owns the requested record)"", ""A denial-of-service attack"", ""A properly configured firewall""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""The app exposes records by ID without checking that the requester is authorized to view them - broken access control (insecure direct object reference). It is a flaw, not encryption, DoS, or firewall behavior.""},

{""id"": ""C5-106"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.1"", ""tags"": [""input-handling""], ""type"": ""spot-flaw"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-web-team-reviews-how-their-app-handles"", ""code"": ""I.   Validates input against an expected format
II.  Inserts raw user input directly into database queries
III. Escapes output before displaying it
IV.  Rejects overly long or malformed input"", ""stem"": ""A web team reviews how their app handles user input. Which practice INTRODUCES a vulnerability?"", ""options"": [""Practice I"", ""Practice III"", ""Practice II"", ""Practice IV""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Inserting raw user input directly into queries (II) enables SQL injection. Validating input, escaping output, and rejecting malformed input are all protective practices.""},

{""id"": ""C5-107"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.2"", ""tags"": [""rbac""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""in-role-based-access-control-rbac-permissions-are-granted"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""In role-based access control (RBAC), permissions are granted based on:"", ""options"": [""The user's seniority in years only"", ""The user's assigned role within the organization"", ""Whichever files the user requests first"", ""The time of day the user logs in""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""RBAC assigns permissions to roles, and users receive access according to their role. Seniority, request order, and time of day are not how RBAC determines permissions.""},

{""id"": ""C5-108"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.2"", ""tags"": [""separation-of-duties""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-company-requires-that-the-employee-who-submits"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A company requires that the employee who submits a payment cannot also be the one who approves it. This control is BEST described as:"", ""options"": [""Single sign-on"", ""Separation of duties"", ""Defense in depth"", ""Security through obscurity""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Requiring two different people for a sensitive transaction is separation of duties, which prevents one person from completing a fraudulent action alone. The other terms describe different concepts.""},

{""id"": ""C5-109"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.2"", ""tags"": [""data-access""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-practices-support-the-principle-of-least-privilege"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which practices support the principle of least privilege for DATA access?

I.   Granting employees access only to the data their job requires
II.  Reviewing and revoking access when roles change
III. Giving all staff read/write access to every database for convenience"", ""options"": [""I and II only"", ""II and III only"", ""I and III only"", ""I, II, and III""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""Granting only job-necessary access (I) and revoking access on role change (II) implement least privilege. Universal read/write access (III) is the opposite of least privilege.""},

{""id"": ""C5-110"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.2"", ""tags"": [""data-classification""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""medium"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-do-organizations-classify-data-into-levels-such"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why do organizations classify data into levels such as public, internal, and confidential?"", ""options"": [""To make all data publicly downloadable"", ""To delete data automatically each night"", ""To apply protection appropriate to each data's sensitivity"", ""To avoid ever needing encryption""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Data classification lets an organization apply controls proportional to sensitivity, focusing strong protections where they matter most. It is not about publishing, auto-deleting, or avoiding encryption.""},

{""id"": ""C5-111"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.3"", ""tags"": [""symmetric""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""in-symmetric-encryption-such-as-aes-the-same"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""In symmetric encryption such as AES, the SAME key is used to:"", ""options"": [""Encrypt with one key and decrypt with a different key"", ""Only hash data, never reverse it"", ""Both encrypt and decrypt the data"", ""Sign data without any key""], ""answer"": 2, ""explanation"": ""Symmetric encryption uses a single shared key for both encryption and decryption. Using different keys for each operation describes asymmetric encryption, and hashing is one-way.""},

{""id"": ""C5-112"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.3"", ""tags"": [""hashing-vs-encryption""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""what-is-the-key-difference-between-hashing-and"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""What is the KEY difference between hashing and encryption?"", ""options"": [""Hashing is reversible but encryption is not"", ""Hashing is one-way and not meant to be reversed
column2: encryption is reversible with the correct key"", ""Hashing requires two keys
column3: encryption requires none"", ""They are identical processes""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Hashing is a one-way function used for integrity and password storage and is not meant to be reversed, while encryption is designed to be reversed with the correct key. The other statements reverse or confuse these properties.""},

column1: {""id"": ""C5-113"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.3"", ""tags"": [""password-storage""], ""type"": ""scenario"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""a-database-stores-user-passwords-which-storage-approach"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""A database stores user passwords. Which storage approach is the MOST secure?"", ""options"": [""Store passwords as plaintext for easy recovery"", ""Store salted hashes of passwords, never the passwords themselves"", ""Store passwords encrypted with a key kept next to the database"", ""Store passwords reversed character by character""], ""answer"": 1, ""explanation"": ""Storing salted hashes means the original passwords are never kept and identical passwords produce different hashes, resisting precomputed attacks. Plaintext is unsafe, a key stored beside the data offers little protection, and reversing characters is trivial to undo.""},

{""id"": ""C5-114"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.3"", ""tags"": [""salt""], ""type"": ""concept"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""why-is-a-unique-salt-added-to-each"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Why is a unique 'salt' added to each password before hashing?"", ""options"": [""So identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating precomputed (rainbow table) attacks"", ""To make the password shorter"", ""To encrypt the network connection"", ""To allow the password to be recovered in plaintext""], ""answer"": 0, ""explanation"": ""A unique salt ensures identical passwords hash to different values, defeating rainbow-table lookups. It does not shorten passwords, encrypt connections, or make hashes reversible.""},

{""id"": ""C5-115"", ""unit"": 5, ""topic"": ""5.3"", ""tags"": [""encryption-at-rest""], ""type"": ""multi-correct"", ""difficulty"": ""hard"", ""featured"": true, ""slug"": ""which-statements-about-encrypting-stored-data-at-rest"", ""code"": """", ""stem"": ""Which statements about encrypting stored data ('at rest') are TRUE?

I.   It protects confidentiality if storage media are stolen
